bibl.title: Hearing in Laboratory Animals: Strain Differences and Nonauditory Effects of Noise

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: This summary demonstrates that noise can alter, either directly or indirectly, virtually every major system studied in biomedical research.

span.label: nonauditory effects of noise in laboratory animals
span.quote: The broad systemic effects of noise exposure include changes in endocrine and cardiovascular function, sleep–wake cycle disturbances, seizure susceptibility, and an array of behavioral changes.

span.label: review
span.quote: This article reviews some of the basic strain and species differences in hearing and outlines how the acoustic environment affects different mammals.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Noise engages the sympathetic branch of the autonomic nervous system, producing a generic stress response like that of other stressors
span.quote: Noise activates the sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system, producing a stress response with physiological characteristics similar to those triggered by other sensory and psychosocial stimuli (35, 46, 163, 164).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Chronic noise keeps the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activated, so circulating stress hormones stay abnormally high and cause downstream organ-system problems
span.quote: The almost universal finding that noise increases stress hormone levels suggests that chronic noise-induced activation of the HPA axis might cause a variety of problems because of abnormally high levels of circulating stress hormones.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Sensory input sets the organism's arousal level, and noise reaches many organ systems through that arousal pathway
span.quote: A key function of sensory systems input is to maintain an ethologically appropriate level of arousal (123), and noise affects a number of organ systems and can impact nearly every area of biomedical and behavioral research via this mechanism.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Even quiet background sound masks conspecific communication signals, impairing the animal's ability to communicate
span.quote: Under this scenario, even a relatively quiet acoustic signal might impair an organism's ability to communicate, perhaps explaining some of the adverse effects of noise (37).

span.label: The review is explicitly selective rather than exhaustive on the auditory-system literature.
span.note: what this limits: the coverage of the review: THIS OVERVIEW IS NOT AN EXHAUSTIVE SUMMARY OF THE LITERATURE CONCERNING THE EFFECTS OF NOISE ON THE AUDITORY SYSTEM
span.quote: This overview is not an exhaustive summary of the literature concerning the effects of noise on the auditory system.

span.label: Much of the nonauditory evidence comes from human subjects, and its generalisability to animals is not established.
span.note: what this limits: the transfer of the nonauditory evidence: THE DEGREE TO WHICH SOME OF THESE OBSERVATIONS CAN BE GENERALIZED TO ANIMALS REMAINS TO BE DETERMINED
span.quote: The degree to which some of these observations can be generalized to animals remains to be determined.

span.label: The acoustic environment produced by different caging systems has not been compared, so cage-level exposure is not known.
span.note: what this limits: any cross-facility comparison of auditory work: FURTHER RESEARCH IS NEEDED TO COMPARE THE ACOUSTIC ENVIRONMENT AS A FUNCTION OF DIFFERENT CAGING CONDITIONS - the housing noise environment is an uncontrolled variable
span.quote: Further research is needed to compare the acoustic environment as a function of different caging conditions, especially given the increased use of isolator caging.

span.label: The evidence base is not yet strong enough to support precise noise guidelines.
span.note: what this limits: the derivation of noise guidelines: BEFORE MORE PRECISE GUIDELINES CAN BE DEVELOPED, MORE SYSTEMATIC RESEARCH ON NOISE AFFECTS IS NECESSARY
span.quote: However, before more precise guidelines can be developed, more systematic research on noise affects is necessary.

span.label: Strains used as standard laboratory animals go progressively deaf for genetic reasons, with secondary effects reaching brain neurochemistry and social behaviour.
span.note: what this limits: any mouse experiment using C57BL/6, DBA/2 or BALB/c, whether or not it concerns hearing: these strains experience genetically determined progressive hearing loss with secondary changes from brain neurochemistry to social behaviour
span.quote: For example, several inbred mouse strains commonly used in biomedical research (e.g., C57BL/6, DBA/2, and BALB/c) experience a genetically determined, progressive hearing loss that can lead to secondary changes in systems ranging from brain neurochemistry to social behavior.

span.label: The review's recommendation is precautionary rather than evidential: assume the exposure could cause any of the effects described.
span.note: what this limits: noise levels in an animal facility as a controlled variable: the review states researchers should ASSUME noise exposure could cause any or all of the described changes, across a wide variety of biomedical research areas
span.quote: researchers and animal care workers should assume that noise exposure could cause any or all of the changes described, potentially impacting a wide variety of biomedical research areas.

span.label: The review defines its central term as broadly as possible, by stipulation.
span.note: what this limits: the scope of 'noise' in this review: it is stipulated as any sound in the environment, so the effects described are not restricted to loud or aversive sound
span.quote: For the purpose of this review, noise can be defined broadly as any sound in the environment.

span.label: The central term is defined by stipulation and as broadly as possible - 'noise can be defined broadly as any sound in the environment' - so the review's scope is set by a definitional choice rather than by a property of the sounds, and every claim about 'noise' inherits that breadth.
span.quote: For the purpose of this review, noise can be defined broadly as any sound in the environment

span.label: noise
span.quote: For the purpose of this review, noise can be defined broadly as any sound in the environment.

span.label: temporary threshold shift
span.quote: Noise overexposure can cause a loss of hearing that is either temporary (temporary threshold shift; TTS) or sometimes permanent (permanent threshold shift; PTS).

span.label: strain
span.quote: Both researchers and laboratory animal facility personnel should be aware of both strain and species differences in hearing in order to minimize potentially confounding variables in their research

span.label: C57BL/6
span.quote: For example, several inbred mouse strains commonly used in biomedical research (e.g., C57BL/6, DBA/2, and BALB/c) experience a genetically determined, progressive hearing loss that can lead to secondary changes in systems ranging from brain neurochemistry to social behavior. Both researchers and laboratory animal facility personnel should be aware of both strain and species differences in hearing in order to minimize potentially confounding variables in their research and to aid in the interpretation of data

span.label: hearing loss
span.quote: For example, several inbred mouse strains commonly used in biomedical research (e.g., C57BL/6, DBA/2, and BALB/c) experience a genetically determined, progressive hearing loss that can lead to secondary changes in systems ranging from brain neurochemistry to social behavior. Both researchers and laboratory animal facility personnel should be aware of both strain and species differences in hearing in order to minimize potentially confounding variables in their research and to aid in the interpretation of data

span.label: hearing loss - TEMPORARY: a temporary threshold shift, which recovers
span.quote: Noise overexposure can cause a loss of hearing that is either temporary (temporary threshold shift; TTS) or sometimes permanent (permanent threshold shift; PTS).

span.label: noise - stipulated for this review as ANY sound in the environment, rather than as unwanted or damaging sound
span.quote: For the purpose of this review, noise can be defined broadly as any sound in the environment.

span.label: noise - stipulated for this review as ANY SOUND IN THE ENVIRONMENT, defined 'broadly' and by fiat rather than by acoustic or perceptual criteria, which is what lets the review range from cage ventilation to conspecific calls
span.quote: For the purpose of this review, noise can be defined broadly as any sound in the environment

span.label: builds-on → Babisch (reference 6), a recent review of noise effects in humans concluding that noise is an established psychosocial stressor
span.quote: We echo this sentiment as it relates to laboratory animals.

span.label: strain —causes→ hearing loss
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — THE STANDARD LABORATORY ANIMAL HAS THE CONFOUND BUILT IN. 'several inbred mouse strains COMMONLY USED IN BIOMEDICAL RESEARCH (e.g., C57BL/6, DBA/2, and BALB/c) experience a GENETICALLY DETERMINED, PROGRESSIVE HEARING LOSS that can lead to secondary changes in systems ranging from brain neurochemistry to social behavior.' The animals chosen as the standard are not typical on the variable, and the consequences reach fields that never measure it - the same shape as the WEIRD-sample problem, in a different kingdom.
span.quote: For example, several inbred mouse strains commonly used in biomedical research (e.g., C57BL/6, DBA/2, and BALB/c) experience a genetically determined, progressive hearing loss that can lead to secondary changes in systems ranging from brain neurochemistry to social behavior. Both researchers and laboratory animal facility personnel should be aware of both strain and species differences in hearing in order to minimize potentially confounding variables in their research and to aid in the interpretation of data

span.label: hearing loss —part-of→ C57BL/6
span.quote: For example, several inbred mouse strains commonly used in biomedical research (e.g., C57BL/6, DBA/2, and BALB/c) experience a genetically determined, progressive hearing loss that can lead to secondary changes in systems ranging from brain neurochemistry to social behavior. Both researchers and laboratory animal facility personnel should be aware of both strain and species differences in hearing in order to minimize potentially confounding variables in their research and to aid in the interpretation of data

span.label: noise —contrasted-with→ strain
span.note: differs in: WHETHER THE VARIABLE IS A NUISANCE OR AN INSTRUMENT, and the paper offers both readings in one sentence: recognise noise 'in order to either MINIMIZE noise as a confounding variable or, in some cases, TO USE NOISE EXPERIMENTALLY as a stress manipulation'. The same environmental fact is a threat to one design and the manipulation of another · strength of the relation: 0.7
span.quote: Whatever the area of study, from immune response to social behavior, the potential impact of environmental noise on the process should be recognized in order to either minimize noise as a confounding variable or, in some cases, to use noise experimentally as a stress manipulation

span.label: The authors' own recording inside a rat shoebox cage in a normal housing room put baseline background noise at about 42 dB SPL across the spectrum.
span.quote: Baseline levels of noise across the spectrum appear to be around 42 dB SPL.

span.label: A routine husbandry action, snapping a wire-top lid onto a shoebox cage, generates a near-100 dB SPL low-frequency impulse with roughly 80 dB SPL of energy extending into the ultrasonic range up to 40 kHz.
span.quote: For example, the common practice of simply snapping a wire-top cage lid to a plastic shoebox cage can produce an intense low-frequency noise impulse of nearly 100 dB SPL, with energy of about 80 dB SPL at frequencies up to 40 kHz (Fig. 2).

span.label: Most facility noise traces to two sources: staff activity itself, and animals vocalising or banging cages in reaction to people being present.
span.quote: These findings suggest that the majority of noise in animal facilities is due to two leading sources: the direct activity of personnel using the facility and the increased activity (vocalization. cage rattling or banging) of animals in response to the presence and actions of people.

span.label: DBA/2 mice begin losing hearing at about two weeks of age and are profoundly deaf by three to four months, so strain choice determines what the animal can hear.
span.quote: For example, relative to other strains, DBA/2 mice demonstrate substantial hearing loss beginning at the onset of hearing (around 2 weeks of age) and progressing rapidly until they are profoundly deaf by around 3 to 4 months of age (51, 152, 200).

span.label: Two common rat strains differ in opposite directions by roughly 20 dB: F344 hear low frequencies better and FBN hybrids hear high frequencies better.
span.quote: F344s show approximately 20 dB better hearing at low frequencies (4 kHz) whereas FBNs show approximately 20 dB better hearing at higher frequencies (32 kHz; 187).

span.label: Nonauditory effects appear well below the 85 dB guideline, with chronic exposure to as little as 65 dB(A) sufficient to induce them.
span.quote: Ising and Kruppa (94) indicated that chronic exposure to as little as 65 dB(A) of noise can induce a variety of nonauditory effects.

span.label: Rearing animals in the constant white-noise masking background recommended by some facilities may itself harm auditory development by masking vocalisations and other natural input.
span.quote: The suggestion from this work is that rearing animals in a constant white noise, masking background (which is being recommended in some animal facilities) might have negative consequences for normal development of the auditory system by effectively masking out the normal input to the ear from vocalizations and other sources.

span.label: noise
span.quote: For the purpose of this review, noise can be defined broadly as any sound in the environment.

span.label: temporary threshold shift (TTS) and permanent threshold shift (PTS)
span.term: temporary threshold shift (TTS) and permanent threshold shift (PTS)
span.quote: Noise overexposure can cause a loss of hearing that is either temporary (temporary threshold shift; TTS) or sometimes permanent (permanent threshold shift; PTS).

span.label: spectral analysis
span.quote: Spectral analysis refers to the process of specifying the amplitude, frequency, and phase relationships of the sinusoidal components of a complex waveform.

span.label: dB sound pressure level (SPL)
span.quote: The most common way to express the amplitude of a sound in dB is relative to the international sound pressure standard of 20 µPa. This is referred to as dB sound pressure level (SPL).

span.label: acoustic priming
span.quote: In a related phenomenon known as acoustic priming, exposure to just a few seconds of loud noise during a critical period early in life can cause seizure-resistant mice to develop a pronounced susceptibility (81).

span.label: frequency
span.quote: The frequency of a sinusoid refers to the number of repetitions of the sinusoid that take place in 1 sec.

span.label: environmental noise as an unintended, confounding variable in animal research
span.term: environmental noise as an unintended, confounding variable in animal research
span.quote: Noise is involved in thousands of scientific studies, not as a purposefully manipulated independent variable, but as an unintended environmental variable that can in some cases confound the data.

span.label: species and strain of the exposed animal
span.term: species and strain of the exposed animal
span.quote: These changes are determined partly by species and strain; partly by noise intensity level, duration, predictability, and other characteristics of the sound; and partly by animal history and exposure context.

span.label: husbandry environment variables (lighting, temperature, humidity, airborne particles, food and water)
span.term: husbandry environment variables (lighting, temperature, humidity, airborne particles, food and water)
span.quote: Laboratory animal facilities typically make great efforts to control environmental variables such as lighting, temperature, humidity, airborne particles, and food and water supply (209).

span.label: 42 dB SPL — Baseline background noise level measured inside a rat cage in a standard animal housing room
span.quote: Baseline levels of noise across the spectrum appear to be around 42 dB SPL.

span.label: nearly 100 dB SPL — Peak low-frequency impulse produced by attaching a wire-top lid to a shoebox cage
span.quote: For example, the common practice of simply snapping a wire-top cage lid to a plastic shoebox cage can produce an intense low-frequency noise impulse of nearly 100 dB SPL, with energy of about 80 dB SPL at frequencies up to 40 kHz (Fig. 2).

span.label: ≥ 85 dB — Sound pressure level above which prolonged chronic exposure is recommended to be treated as capable of causing permanent cochlear hearing loss
span.quote: As a result of human and laboratory animal studies, current recommendations are that chronic exposure to noise levels at ≥ 85 dB sound pressure level (SPL) for any prolonged period of time can cause permanent hearing loss through cochlear damage (131).

span.label: 75% — Proportion of acoustically primed CBA mice that seized and died on re-exposure to the 123-dB noise
span.quote: For example, if CBA mice (which hear normally and are not susceptible to audiogenic seizures) are exposed to a 123-dB noise for 2 min when they are 24 to 42 days old, that same exposure repeated 5 days later leads to seizures and death in 75% of the animals (80).

span.label: more than 90% — Share of mammals used in research that are mice, whose hearing extends into the ultrasonic range beyond human hearing
span.quote: The more commonly used laboratory animals, such as mice, which make up more than 90% of mammals used in research (120), have hearing with frequency sensitivity in the ultrasonic range (≥ 80,000 Hz), far beyond the range of the human ear (20 to 20.000 Hz).

span.label: 60 episodes/0.5 h at ≥ 90 dB — Rate of loud noise episodes recorded in animal facilities in the morning, rising above 100 dB in the evening
span.quote: Pfaff and Stacker (148) recorded noise levels in animal facilities and found approximately 60 episodes/0.5 h at ≥ 90 dB in the morning and > 60 episodes/0.5 h at ≥100 dB in the evening.
